description: We are friends brought together by technology. Our goal for this event is to dive headfirst into the challenges, gain as much knowledge as possible, and learn a great deal through hands-on practice!
summary:
Imagine it is day od a 900-day mission, on the way to Mars. Earth is up to 22 minutes away, so Dr. Okafor, the crew medical officer, leads every medical decision on board.
Commander Silva wakes up with a body temperature of 37.6 °C. Astro Health marks it "Watch" and tells her what to do: drink 250 ml of water and rest for 30 minutes. Once she ticks both steps, her Astroskin shirt takes a new reading on its own.
Her other readings arrive live, with nothing to type: 7 h 10 min of sleep, 116/76 mmHg, 98% SpO₂ and 1.9 of 2.5 L of water. A 3D astronaut shows each one on the suit. Her readiness is 86/100, down 3 points since yesterday but still above the 80 needed for a spacewalk. When she asks "How is my health today?", the assistant answers with these exact numbers and shows where to see them. At 08:00 UTC, the chat reminds her to take vitamin D.
Meanwhile, Dr. Okafor's panel puts Eng. Tanaka first: readiness 58 and a fever. If any reading reaches "Act now", a voice guides the rescue step by step and alerts the crew with the location.
Offline, free and accessible, Astro Health turns data into decisions when Earth is too far away.
details:
Astro Health is a web app for astronauts and the crew medical officer. It tracks health before, during and after missions to the space station, the Moon and Mars. Each screen shows only what matters in that phase.

Continuous monitoring.

  • No typing: the Astroskin shirt (heart rate, blood pressure, SpO₂, breathing, temperature and sleep), the water dispenser and the exercise machines (ARED, treadmill and cycle) send data on their own. The app updates numbers and charts every 5 seconds.
  • The only vital sign typed by hand: blood glucose, and only when the glucometer is not connected over Bluetooth. Mood and symptoms are logged by the astronaut.

3D astronaut.

  • Sensor points: NASA's EMU suit shows 8 points colored by status. Tapping a point opens its current value, the last 24 hours and what to do.
  • Symptoms: tapping a body region logs a symptom with a 1–5 intensity, and each level comes with fixed guidance.

Nausea mode.

  • When nausea or vomiting is logged, the screen shows only the essentials, with no animation and a "what helps now" bar.

Voice-guided emergency.

  • How it starts: when a vital sign reaches "Act now", or with the SOS button.
  • What happens: the voice reads the values and each step of the guide, alerts the crew in real time and shows where the emergency is on the habitat map and accepts the commands "next", "repeat" and "help".
  • CPR: includes a metronome set to 110 compressions per minute and a timer

"Ask" assistant.

  • How to ask: pick a suggestion, type or speak.
  • What it answers:What it answers: it uses real data (health today, weekly trends, readiness, sleep, tasks, medication) and passages from the app’s guides, always with ‘where to see it in the app'.

Messages and goals.

  • Health chat: reminders for tasks, medication (vitamin D and the contraceptive pill) and exams arrive as messages, with no pop-ups.
  • Daily goals: water, exercise, sleep and a mood check-in, with private achievements.

Doctor's panel.

  • Crew: health records, alerts sorted by urgency with decision guides, and review of the neck ultrasound the astronaut sends.
  • Before flight: scheduling of pre-flight exams.

Modules by sex.

  • Women's health: cycle plan, pill and its supply, urinary symptoms and preparation for the flight.
  • Men's health: early alerts for vision problems (SANS), noise exposure and hearing tests, and radiation and fertility.

Fine-grained privacy.

  • Choice by data type: each person decides who sees each type of data: flight surgeon, crew medical officer or researchers (with consent).
  • Mission control: only sees whether each astronaut is ‘fit for duty’ or not.

Benefits that solve current problems

  • Autonomy far from Earth: with up to 22 minutes of delay, the app gives immediate guidance that is offline and deterministic.
  • No manual logging of vital signs: data comes from the sensors, so astronauts neither lose time nor make typing errors.
  • Every status says how to get back to normal: each "Watch" shows "Back to normal when…" and the steps to follow.
  • Hands-free emergency: voice, captions and spoken commands, with an automatic alert to the crew.
  • The gap in women's data: only about 75 women have flown to space. The women's module addresses their needs and lets them donate anonymous data to research.
  • Less visual clutter: notifications in a chat, nausea mode, and one test for every element on screen: "does it help the person act on their own health in this phase?".

Intended impact

  • Medical autonomy: support crews on long missions such as Artemis and Mars, in line with NASA's Human Research Program.
  • Early detection: Early detection: help flag the first signs of risks such as SANS (Spaceflight Associated Neuro-ocular Syndrome), jugular vein thrombosis, bone loss and radiation effects.
  • More inclusive science: collect more data on women’s health in space.
  • Use on Earth: the same model (sensors, offline guidance and accessibility) serves isolated places such as offshore platforms, Antarctic stations and remote areas.

Tools, languages, hardware and software

  • Languages: vanilla JavaScript (no frameworks), HTML5 and CSS3, with the BEM methodology and design tokens.
    • Three.js r170 (3D, with GLTFLoader, DRACOLoader and RoomEnvironment);
    • Firebase JS SDK (Firestore and anonymous Auth, for real-time alerts).
  • Hardware considered: Astroskin shirt, radiation and acoustic dosimeters, Bluetooth glucometer, portable ultrasound, OCT, SLAMMD (mass measurement without gravity) and the ARED, T2 and CEVIS machines.
  • Infrastructure: Firebase Hosting (free Spark plan) and a back end modeled in Supabase/PostgreSQL. The App.records layer already uses the database tables and columns.
  • Quality: Playwright (regression tests at 414 and 1280 px) and axe-core (zero accessibility violations in light and dark themes).
  • Design: Figma/FigJam (UX research) and the official Space Apps 2026 visual standards.

Creative aspects

  • A clickable 3D astronaut as the interface for the body, with regions that light up when touched or hovered over.
  • Nausea mode as "space accessibility".
  • A voice-driven emergency guide that does not mistake its own speech for a command.
  • An assistant that answers with real numbers without generative AI: safe, predictable and offline.
  • A health chat instead of pop-ups.
  • Surface contexts: base and rover on the Moon and Mars, with a higher readiness score required on the rover (85 instead of 80), because help from the base is 40 minutes away.

Factors the team considered

Research came first. Before writing any code, we researched the whole picture:

  • how astronauts train before a mission;
  • how pre-flight, in-flight and post-flight exams are done today, and how health is monitored on board now;
  • what causes the most problems for astronauts (the pain points);
  • how the body reacts differently in women and men;
  • how life and medical support change between Earth, the space station, the Moon and Mars.

We mapped these findings in a UX study in FigJam. They decided which screens exist and what each one shows.

We put accessibility and usability first. We designed the interface for WCAG 2.2 AA and Nielsen's 10 heuristics from the start, not as a final check:

  • status shown with icons and text, never color alone;
  • full keyboard navigation;
  • large touch targets;
  • captions for every spoken word.

We also created a "nausea mode" for space sickness, and made sure every warning tells the astronaut how to get back to normal.

We worked in a clear front-end, back-end and QA flow:

  • Front end: pure JavaScript with the BEM methodology and a design system based on the official Space Apps brand, built mobile first and offline first. We added only a few free, locally hosted libraries (Three.js for the 3D astronaut, Firebase for real-time crew alerts).
  • Back end: we modeled the database in Supabase/PostgreSQL, and the app saves data with the same tables and columns.
  • QA: the main features were covered by automated tests on phone and desktop screen sizes, including accessibility checks in light and dark themes.

We defined a file architecture for performance. Shared code lives in assets/, each page in its own folder, and common parts are generated by one script. This keeps the code lean and reusable, loads heavy parts only when needed, and targets a PageSpeed score of 90 or higher.

We prioritized safety. No AI decides on medical care. The assistant and the emergency voice use fixed, verified texts with the real measured values, always show where the information comes from, and display "Not a medical device".

We worked as a team. We split the tasks so no one carried too much, and every member of the team contributed equally.
